chunks.text: AyurIP Sahayak — Ayurveda, Traditional Knowledge & Intellectual Property Knowledge Base Table of Contents AyurIP Sahayak — Ayurveda, Traditional Knowledge & Intellectual Property Knowledge Base A structured reference document for an AI-powered research assistant on Ayurveda, Traditional Knowledge (TK), and Intellectual Property (IP) protection in India. Document type: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) knowledge-base source Scope: Educational and legal-awareness reference. Not legal advice. Not medical advice. Verification notice: Wherever this document states a law, rule, statistic, or institutional fact, it should be re-checked against the current official source before being relied upon, because legal provisions, fees, procedures, and institutional details change over time. How to use this document This document is organized into twelve numbered sections, each self-contained so that a retrieval system can return an individual section or sub-section as a complete answer unit.

Each section ends with a short factual summary and a “Sources / Further Reading” list. A consolidated glossary of over 100 terms appears at the end (Section 12). Throughout this document: • [VERIFY] marks a fact that is time-sensitive, numeric, or otherwise likely to change, and that should be confirmed against an official source before use. • Traditional claim marks a statement describing what Ayurvedic texts or practice say, without asserting that modern science has confirmed it. • Scientific evidence marks a statement about what peer-reviewed or regulatory scientific evaluation has found.

Ayurveda (from Sanskrit āyus, “life” or “longevity,” and veda, “knowledge” or “science”) is one of the world’s oldest documented systems of medicine and wellbeing, originating on the Indian subcontinent. It is recognized in India as one of the officially supported Indian Systems of Medicine, alongside Yoga, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa, and Homoeopathy, collectively administered under the Ministry of AYUSH. Traditional claim: Ayurveda describes itself as a comprehensive system covering diet, lifestyle, herbal and mineral formulations, detoxification and rejuvenation procedures (Panchakarma), surgery (as historically described in the Sushruta Samhita), and preventive and promotive health practices, aimed at maintaining balance between mind, body, and environment. Scientific evidence: Modern biomedical science evaluates Ayurvedic concepts and formulations using its own separate frameworks (pharmacology, clinical trials, toxicology).

Modern biomedical science evaluates Ayurvedic concepts and formulations using its own separate frameworks (pharmacology, clinical trials, toxicology). Some individual Ayurvedic herbs and formulations have been studied using modern scientific methods with mixed and formulation-specific results; Ayurveda as a whole system has not been validated or invalidated as a single unit by modern science, because its foundational concepts (doshas, dhatus) are not framework-equivalent to biomedical categories. Claims of efficacy for any specific condition should be verified against current peer-reviewed literature and regulatory assessments rather than assumed from tradition alone.

• Ayurvedic concepts are traceable to ancient Sanskrit textual traditions, with foundational compilations conventionally dated to roughly the first millennium BCE through the early centuries CE, though exact dating of oral- to-written transmission is debated among historians. • Ayurveda developed alongside other Indian intellectual traditions (philosophy, surgery, chemistry/alchemy known as Rasashastra) and was transmitted through teacher-student (guru-shishya) lineages, temple and monastic institutions, and family/community practice. • During the colonial period, institutional support for Ayurveda in India declined relative to Western biomedicine; post-independence India took steps to formally recognize and regulate Ayurveda through dedicated statutes, education boards, and eventually a dedicated ministry (Ministry of AYUSH, elevated to a full ministry in 2014 [VERIFY]).

• Today Ayurveda is practiced in India under statutory regulation (registered practitioners, accredited colleges) and has also spread internationally as a complementary/alternative medicine system, subject to the medical-practice and product-safety laws of each country.

A number of other texts (e.g., Madhava Nidana, Sharangadhara Samhita, Bhava Prakasha) are also considered important classical sources, particularly for diagnosis, formulation methods ( Bhaishajya Kalpana), and later systematizations. Relevance to IP and TK work: These texts, along with regional and vernacular Ayurvedic literature, are the single most important category of documentary evidence used to demonstrate that a given herb, formulation, or use is traditional knowledge and therefore prior art for patent purposes (see Section 3 on TKDL and Section 5 on Patents).
The following are traditional Ayurvedic concepts. They are described here as they appear in Ayurvedic theory; they are not biomedical diagnostic categories.

Traditional claim: Ayurveda describes three fundamental physiological principles called doshas, said to govern bodily and mental functions: • Vata — associated with movement, the nervous system, circulation, and elimination; traditionally linked to the elements air and space/ether. • Pitta — associated with metabolism, digestion, and transformation; traditionally linked to the elements fire and water. • Kapha — associated with structure, lubrication, and stability; traditionally linked to the elements earth and water. Ayurvedic theory holds that each individual has a unique baseline proportion of the three doshas and that disease arises from imbalance among them. This is a traditional explanatory framework, not a scientifically validated physiological model in the biomedical sense.

Traditional claim: Dhatus are the seven traditional “tissues” said to sustain the body: Rasa (plasma/nutrient fluid), Rakta (blood), Mamsa (muscle), Meda (fat), Asthi (bone), Majja (marrow/nervous tissue), and Shukra (reproductive tissue).

Traditional claim: Malas are the traditional waste products of metabolism — principally Purisha (feces), Mutra (urine), and Sweda (sweat) — whose proper elimination is considered necessary for health.

Traditional claim: Prakriti refers to an individual’s inherent constitutional type, determined (according to Ayurvedic theory) at conception by the relative proportion of the three doshas, and considered relatively fixed for life. Ayurvedic practice traditionally uses assessment of Prakriti to guide individualized dietary and lifestyle recommendations. This is a traditional classificatory concept and is distinct from, and should not be confused with, genetic or genomic classification in modern biology.

chunks.section: 1.6 Common Ayurvedic Formulations and Traditional Preparation
chunks.text: Methods Ayurvedic pharmaceutics (Bhaishajya Kalpana) traditionally classifies preparations by method, including (illustrative, non-exhaustive): • Churna — fine herbal powder. • Kwatha/Kashaya — decoction, prepared by boiling herbal material in water. • Arishta/Asava — fermented liquid preparations. • Ghrita — medicated clarified butter (ghee) preparations. • Taila — medicated oil preparations. • Vati/Gutika — tablets or pills. • Bhasma — a category of processed mineral/metal preparations subjected to specific traditional purification (Shodhana) and incineration (Marana) processes; because these can involve heavy metals (e.g., mercury, lead), they are subject to specific quality-control and regulatory scrutiny in modern manufacture, and safety depends heavily on correct processing and regulatory compliance. chunks.section: 1.6 Common Ayurvedic Formulations and Traditional Preparation
chunks.text: Distinguishing traditional knowledge from modern scientific evidence (general principle for this entire document): A traditional preparation method or use being centuries old does not, by itself, establish that the preparation is safe, effective, or free of contamination by modern regulatory standards. Conversely, a preparation being traditional does not mean it lacks value — it means the claim should be evaluated on its own evidentiary merits (toxicology, clinical data, regulatory approval) rather than by appeal to tradition or by dismissal of tradition. This distinction is central to Sections 2–5 of this document, which examine how traditional use interacts with patent law (as prior art) rather than with medical claims.

“Traditional Knowledge” (TK) does not have one single, universally binding legal definition, but it is generally understood — including in WIPO’s work — as knowledge, know-how, skills, and practices that are developed, sustained, and passed down from generation to generation within a community, often forming part of its cultural or spiritual identity. TK can relate to agriculture, the environment, healthcare (including Ayurveda and other traditional medicine systems), biodiversity-related knowledge, and traditional/cultural expressions. [VERIFY] Because there is no single global treaty definition of TK currently in force (as opposed to ongoing negotiations — see Section 9), the precise legal scope of “traditional knowledge” can differ between national laws and international discussions. Any project relying on a specific legal definition should identify which law or instrument’s definition is being used.

chunks.section: 2.2 Traditional Knowledge Associated with Biological Resources
chunks.text: A large share of TK relevant to Ayurveda is TK associated with genetic/biological resources — i.e., knowledge about the properties or uses of a specific plant, animal, or microorganism (for example, that a particular plant’s leaves can be used for a particular purpose). This category is significant because: • It sits at the intersection of two international frameworks: intellectual property law (patents) and biodiversity law (access and benefit-sharing, discussed in Section 9). • It is the category most often implicated in “biopiracy” disputes, because a patent claim on a plant-based invention can be undermined or supported by evidence of pre-existing traditional use.

Traditional medicinal knowledge specifically encompasses documented and undocumented knowledge of diagnostic methods, treatments, formulations, and health practices originating in traditional medicine systems (in India, principally Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, and Sowa-Rigpa, alongside Yoga). It exists in two broad forms: 1. Documented traditional knowledge — recorded in classical texts, manuscripts, government publications, or scholarly compilations. This is generally easier to use as documentary prior art in a patent proceeding because it has an identifiable publication date and source. 2. Oral/undocumented traditional knowledge — held within communities, families, or individual practitioners without a formal written record.

2. Oral/undocumented traditional knowledge — held within communities, families, or individual practitioners without a formal written record. This is traditionally harder to use as patent prior art because patent law in most jurisdictions requires evidence of what was “publicly known” or “publicly used” as of a certain date, and undocumented oral knowledge can be difficult to prove or date with the evidentiary certainty patent offices require.

Community knowledge refers to TK held collectively by an identifiable community (e.g., an indigenous or tribal community, or a defined local/traditional occupational group) rather than by an individual inventor. This collective character creates specific legal and ethical challenges: • Conventional IP law (patents, copyright) is generally built around identifiable individual or corporate authorship/inventorship and a fixed term of protection, which fits awkwardly with knowledge that is collectively held, continuously evolving, and intended to be perpetual rather than time-limited. • This mismatch is a central reason why specialized “sui generis” (custom-built) legal approaches to protecting TK have been proposed and, in some countries, adopted, rather than relying solely on existing IP categories (see Section 9).

chunks.section: 2.5 Oral and Documented Traditional Knowledge — Why the Distinction
chunks.text: Matters for IP The oral/documented distinction (introduced in 2.3) has direct legal consequences: • For defensive protection (stopping wrongful patents), documented TK is far more useful because it can be cited as prior art with a verifiable date and source (this is the entire logic behind TKDL — see Section 3). • For positive protection (giving TK holders enforceable rights over their own knowledge), documentation can sometimes cut both ways — it makes the knowledge easier to prove, but publishing knowledge that was previously restricted or sacred can also mean giving up practical control over it, since

“Biopiracy” is a widely used but legally informal term (it does not appear as a defined term in most national statutes) referring to situations where biological resources and/or associated traditional knowledge are accessed, used, or patented — typically by a foreign company, research institution, or government — without adequate prior informed consent from, or benefit-sharing with, the country or community that is the source of the resource or knowledge. Common features cited in biopiracy disputes include: • Patents claiming a “new” use, extract, or method that closely tracks a pre- existing traditional use. • Access to biological material or associated knowledge without the consent required under applicable biodiversity-access law. • Commercialization proceeding without any agreed benefit-sharing arrangement with the country of origin or knowledge-holding community.

“Misappropriation” in this context generally refers to the unauthorized taking, use, or commercial exploitation of TK contrary to the customary norms of the community that holds it, or without the legally required consent/benefit-sharing where such requirements exist. Whether a specific instance amounts to misappropriation as a matter of law depends on the applicable jurisdiction’s rules (e.g., India’s Biological Diversity Act — see Section 6) and on the facts of the case; the term is used loosely in policy debate as well as more precisely in specific statutes.

The following are widely discussed as illustrative examples; detailed treatment of the best-documented cases appears in Section 10 (Case Studies). This list only names disputes and does not restate contested details: • The 1995 U.S. patent on the wound-healing use of turmeric (revoked 1997) — see Case Study, Section 10. • The European Patent Office patent on a neem-based fungicide (revoked after opposition, final appeal decision 2005) — see Case Study, Section 10. • The 1997 U.S. patent granted to RiceTec Inc. relating to “Basmati” rice lines (several claims later withdrawn/cancelled) — see Case Study, Section 10.

• The Kani tribe / Jeevani (TBGRI) benefit-sharing arrangement in Kerala, India — an example often cited for both its innovative benefit-sharing model and its later implementation difficulties — see Case Study, Section 10. • The Hoodia gordonii / San peoples benefit-sharing agreement in South Africa — an international (non-Ayurvedic) example of a TK-related access and benefit-sharing dispute and settlement — see Case Study, Section 10. Section 2 Summary Traditional Knowledge is generation-to-generation knowledge without one single binding global legal definition; it includes TK associated with biological resources and traditional medicinal knowledge, held either in documented or oral form, individually or by communities. Unauthorized commercialization of TK-related resources without consent or benefit-sharing is commonly termed biopiracy or misappropriation, and several well-known disputes (detailed in Section 10) have shaped international and Indian policy responses.

The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) is a digital, structured database of publicly available traditional knowledge relating to Indian systems of medicine, created and maintained by India’s Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in collaboration with the Ministry of AYUSH. It converts information from classical and other public-domain texts on Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa, and Yoga into a searchable digital format, classified using a purpose-built classification system (the Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification, TKRC) and translated into multiple languages (English, French, German, Spanish, and Japanese) so that patent examiners in other countries can search and understand it.

TKDL was created in direct response to a recurring problem: patent applications were being filed and, in some cases, granted in other countries for uses of Indian medicinal plants (such as turmeric and neem) that already existed as traditional knowledge in India, but that traditional knowledge had not been accessible to patent examiners in a form they could search — because it existed mainly in Sanskrit, Hindi, Urdu, Arabic, Tamil, and other languages, in texts not indexed in the patent

classification systems examiners normally use. TKDL was designed to close this “language and format” gap so that genuine prior art could be found before a patent is granted, rather than only after (which requires expensive opposition or re- examination proceedings, as happened in the turmeric and neem cases described in Section 10).

• TKDL was established in 2001 by CSIR in collaboration with (what is now) the Ministry of AYUSH. • Its stated core objective is defensive protection: to prevent the wrongful grant of patents on inventions that are, in substance, already part of India’s traditional knowledge, by making that knowledge available as searchable prior art to patent examiners worldwide. • Over time, TKDL has entered into TKDL Access (Non-Disclosure) Agreements with patent offices in multiple countries and regions, allowing examiners at those offices to search the TKDL database (subject to confidentiality restrictions) during examination of relevant applications. • [VERIFY] The exact number of patent offices with TKDL access, and the exact number of formulations/pages digitized, change over time as the collaboration expands; current figures should be obtained from CSIR/TKDL’s own published materials rather than assumed from any single secondary source.

chunks.section: 3.4 How Traditional Knowledge is Documented in TKDL
chunks.text: TKDL’s methodology, at a general level, involves: 1. Identifying source texts already in the public domain (classical Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, and Sowa-Rigpa texts, and Yoga-related texts). 2. Extracting discrete “shlokas”/formulations/statements of use from those texts. 3. Structuring each entry with standardized fields (e.g., ingredient, disease/use category, method of preparation) using the Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification (TKRC), a classification system created specifically because existing international patent classification systems (like the IPC) did not have adequate categories for traditional medicine subject matter. 4. Translating entries into the five languages listed above. 5. Making the database available to partner patent offices under non-disclosure terms (to prevent the underlying traditional knowledge itself from being taken and misused, while still letting examiners use it to identify lack of novelty).

chunks.section: 3.5 How TKDL Helps Prevent Wrongful Patent Claims
chunks.text: TKDL operates as a form of defensive protection (a concept discussed generally in Section 9): rather than seeking to grant TK holders new exclusive rights, it works by

chunks.section: 3.5 How TKDL Helps Prevent Wrongful Patent Claims
chunks.text: ensuring that patent examiners can find pre-existing traditional knowledge as prior art during the routine examination of a patent application. If an examiner finds that the “invention” being claimed is already described in a TKDL entry, that finding can be used to reject the application for lack of novelty or inventive step (see Section 5 on patentability requirements), ideally before a patent is ever granted — avoiding the need for the costly, multi-year opposition or re-examination proceedings that were required in cases like the turmeric and neem patents.

chunks.section: 3.6 Relationship Between TKDL and Patent Examination
chunks.text: • TKDL is a search and reference tool for examiners , not a legal register of ownership and not itself a form of intellectual property protection for the TK it documents. • TKDL does not, by itself, stop a patent office from granting a patent; it depends on the examiner actually searching and correctly applying the TKDL prior art during examination, or on affected parties citing TKDL material during opposition. • Access is generally structured under confidentiality agreements to strike a balance: examiners can use the content to assess novelty, but the traditional knowledge itself (much of which is culturally significant and, in some communities’ view, should not be freely commercially exploited) is not thereby placed in an unrestricted public database beyond what is already public domain.

TKDL is frequently cited internationally, including in WIPO’s Intergovernmental Committee on Intellectual Property and Genetic Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Folklore (IGC), as a model for defensive protection of traditional knowledge, and has influenced discussions in other countries considering similar national TK databases. [VERIFY] Specific claims about numbers of patent applications withdrawn or amended as a direct result of TKDL citations should be sourced from CSIR/TKDL’s own reporting, as such statistics are updated periodically.

Intellectual Property (IP) refers to a category of legally recognized rights over creations of the mind — inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols, names, and certain confidential information — that allow the rights-holder to control specific uses of that creation for a defined period (or, for some categories such as trade secrets and some trademarks, potentially indefinitely provided conditions are maintained). IP rights are territorial (granted and enforced on a country-by-country or region-by-region basis, subject to international treaties that harmonize certain minimum standards).

Exclusive rights granted for an invention that is new, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application, in exchange for public disclosure of how the invention works. Patents are time-limited (20 years from filing in most jurisdictions including India, subject to renewal-fee payment).

Signs (words, logos, sounds, etc. depending on the jurisdiction) capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one enterprise from those of others. Trademarks can, in principle, be renewed indefinitely as long as they remain in use and renewal fees are paid.

Rights automatically arising (in most jurisdictions, without registration) over original literary, artistic, musical, and certain other creative works, protecting the expression of an idea (not the underlying idea, fact, or method itself) for the life of the author plus a further statutory term (commonly 60 years after death in India [VERIFY]).

A sign used on products that originate from a specific geographical location and possess qualities, reputation, or characteristics essentially attributable to that origin (e.g., a specific region’s traditional agricultural product or handicraft). In India, GIs are protected under a dedicated statute rather than as ordinary trademarks (see Section 6).

Confidential business information (formulas, processes, methods) that derives commercial value from not being generally known, protected for as long as secrecy is maintained through reasonable protective measures, rather than through registration.

Protection for the visual/ornamental appearance of a product (shape, configuration, pattern, or ornamentation), as distinct from its functional or technical features (which would instead be the domain of patents).

A specialized (sui generis) form of IP protecting new plant varieties bred by identifiable breeders, distinct from patents, and in India governed by a dedicated statute (see Section 6) that also recognizes farmers’ rights.

chunks.text: Section 4 Summary Intellectual Property comprises several distinct legal categories — patents, trademarks, copyright, geographical indications, trade secrets, industrial designs, and plant variety protection — each protecting a different kind of subject matter under different requirements and for different durations. Understanding these differences is essential before assessing how (or whether) any given piece of Ayurveda-related traditional knowledge can be protected, and by which tool. In simple terms: a patent is a deal between an inventor and the government. The inventor tells the world exactly how their invention works (full public disclosure), and in exchange, the government gives the inventor the exclusive right to stop others from making, using, selling, or importing that invention for a limited time (in India, 20 years from the filing date, subject to renewal fees).

A patent is a statutory, territorial, negative right — it does not itself grant the patentee a positive right to practice the invention (which may still be restricted by other laws), but it grants the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, offering for sale, or importing the patented invention without authorization, within
the jurisdiction that granted the patent, for the statutory term, provided renewal (maintenance) fees are paid.
For an invention to be patentable in most jurisdictions, including India, it generally must satisfy three core requirements plus a sufficiency-of-disclosure requirement:

The invention must not have been disclosed to the public, anywhere in the world, in any form (written, oral, use, or otherwise) before the patent application’s filing date (or valid priority date). Existing disclosures that defeat novelty are called prior art.

The invention must not be obvious to a “person skilled in the art” (a hypothetical knowledgeable-but-not-inventive practitioner in the relevant technical field) in light of the prior art existing at the relevant date. A small, predictable modification of something already known typically fails this requirement.
The invention must be capable of being made or used in some kind of industry, i.e., it must have a practical, working application rather than being purely theoretical or non-functional.

The patent application must describe the invention clearly and completely enough that a person skilled in the art could reproduce it, and must include claims that define the precise scope of protection sought.

chunks.section: 5.4 Patent Exclusions Relevant to Traditional Knowledge (Indian Law)
chunks.text: Section 3 of India’s Patents Act, 1970 lists categories of subject matter that are not considered “inventions” for patent purposes. Provisions particularly relevant to Ayurveda and traditional knowledge include (paraphrased; the exact statutory wording should be checked in the current Act): • Section 3(p): An invention which, in effect, is traditional knowledge or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of a traditionally known component or components, is excluded from patentability. • Section 3(e) (in substance): A mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of the known properties of its components (e.g., simply combining two known substances without a new synergistic or unexpected effect) is generally excluded. • Section 3(d): Restricts patents on the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance that does not result in enhanced efficacy, and on the mere

chunks.section: 5.4 Patent Exclusions Relevant to Traditional Knowledge (Indian Law)
chunks.text: discovery of a new use for a known substance or of a mere new property of a known substance — a provision frequently discussed in the pharmaceutical patenting context generally, and relevant whenever a “new” use is claimed for an already-known (including traditionally known) natural substance. [VERIFY current text — Section 3(d) has been the subject of significant litigation and interpretation, most notably in pharmaceutical-patent case law, and its precise application should be checked against current judicial interpretation.] These provisions mean that, under Indian law, simply “rediscovering” or scientifically re-describing an already-known traditional use of a plant, without adding something genuinely new (such as a novel extraction method producing an unexpected technical effect, a new synergistic combination, or a new industrially useful form), is unlikely to be patentable in India.

chunks.section: 5.5 Why Traditional Knowledge Can Create Problems for Novelty
chunks.text: Traditional knowledge often exists as unwritten, geographically dispersed, or non- English-language public knowledge. This creates a structural problem for patent examination: • Patent examiners generally search structured, indexed databases (patent literature, indexed scientific journals) using keyword and classification searches. • If a traditional use is real prior art but exists only in a Sanskrit manuscript, a regional-language ethnobotanical survey, or undocumented community practice, an examiner using only conventional search tools may not find it — leading to a patent being granted on subject matter that, in substance, was not novel. • This is precisely the gap that resources like TKDL (Section 3) are designed to close, and precisely what happened, before TKDL access agreements matured, in the turmeric and neem cases (Section 10).

“Prior art” is the body of all information that has been made available to the public, in any form, anywhere, before the relevant filing/priority date of a patent application, and that is therefore usable to assess whether a claimed invention is novel and/or inventive. Prior art can include earlier patents and patent applications, scientific journal articles, books (including classical texts such as the Charaka Samhita where genuinely publicly available before the relevant date), conference presentations, product sales, and — depending on jurisdiction and evidentiary standard — sufficiently documented public use or oral disclosure.

Patent examination is the process by which a patent office’s examiner reviews a filed application against the legal requirements (Section 5.3) and against prior art (Section 5.6) to decide whether to grant, reject, or require amendment of the application. Examination typically includes: • A formal check (fees paid, required documents present, formalities complete). • A prior art search (see Section 5.8) conducted by the examiner using patent databases, scientific literature databases, and, where relevant and accessible, specialized resources like TKDL. • Issuance of an examination report (sometimes called a First Examination Report, or FER, in India) raising objections, if any. • An opportunity for the applicant to respond, amend claims, or argue against objections. • A final decision to grant or refuse, which may itself be subject to opposition (Section 5.11) or appeal.

A patent search is a structured search of patent and non-patent literature conducted to identify existing disclosures relevant to a given invention — done by applicants (before filing, to assess patentability and avoid infringing others’ rights), by examiners (during examination), and by third parties (to oppose a granted or pending patent, or to assess “freedom to operate”). Patent search methodology is discussed in detail in Section 7 (Ayurveda-specific workflow) and Section 8 (general search concepts).

chunks.text: 8. Payment of periodic renewal (maintenance) fees to keep the patent in force for its full term.

Opposition is a formal legal mechanism by which a third party can challenge a patent application (pre-grant) or a granted patent (post-grant) before the patent office, typically on grounds such as lack of novelty, lack of inventive step, insufficient disclosure, or — specifically relevant to this document — that the claimed invention falls within an exclusion such as Section 3(p) of the Indian Patents Act (traditional knowledge) or is anticipated by traditional-knowledge prior art. Outside India, similar mechanisms exist under different names (e.g., “opposition” at the European Patent Office, “re-examination” historically and “post-grant/inter partes review” currently at the USPTO [VERIFY current U.S. procedural names, as U.S. post- grant challenge mechanisms have changed over time, e.g., under the America Invents Act]).

Patent infringement occurs when a party, without authorization from the patentee, makes, uses, sells, offers to sell, or imports the patented invention within the territory where the patent is in force, during its term. Infringement analysis in most systems involves comparing the accused product/process against the specific claims of the patent (the numbered statements at the end of the patent document that legally define its scope), not against the patent’s general description. Available remedies typically include injunctions, damages, or an account of profits, subject to the applicable law and court’s discretion. Section 5 Summary A patent requires novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability, plus adequate disclosure. Indian patent law specifically excludes traditional-knowledge-based “inventions” and mere discoveries of new uses/forms of known substances from patentability (Sections 3(p), 3(e), and 3(d) of the Patents Act, 1970).

Traditional knowledge poses a distinctive novelty-search challenge because it is often undocumented or documented outside conventional patent-searchable formats — the exact gap TKDL was built to close. The Indian Patent Office (a constituent office under the Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs & Trade Marks) is responsible for receiving, examining, and granting or refusing patent applications in India, under the Patents Act, 1970 and the Patents Rules. It operates through patent offices located in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, and Chennai, each with defined territorial jurisdiction. chunks.section: 6.2 Controller General of Patents, Designs & Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
chunks.text: The CGPDTM is the senior administrative authority overseeing India’s patent, design, trademark, and (through affiliated offices) geographical indication registries, functioning under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The CGPDTM issues practice manuals, guidelines (including guidelines specifically addressing examination of biotechnology and traditional-knowledge-related applications), and administers the overall IP registration infrastructure.

India’s principal patent statute. It has been substantively amended several times, most significantly in 2005 (to introduce product patent protection for pharmaceuticals, food, and chemicals, in compliance with India’s TRIPS obligations — see Section 9). It contains the core patentability criteria, the exclusions in Section 3 (including the TK-relevant exclusions discussed in Section 5.4), and the procedural framework for application, examination, opposition, and enforcement.

The Patents Rules (currently the Patents Rules, 2003, as periodically amended) set out the detailed procedural requirements under the Patents Act — forms, fees, timelines, and administrative procedures. [VERIFY current rules, as procedural amendments (e.g., relating to fees, timelines, or startup/small-entity concessions) occur periodically and should be checked on the official IP India website.]

chunks.section: 6.5 Biological Diversity Act (and Current Biodiversity Legislation)
chunks.text: India’s biodiversity-access law is the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended by the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 (notified via Gazette publication in August 2023). Its stated objectives are conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from the use of biological resources and associated traditional knowledge.

chunks.section: 6.5 Biological Diversity Act (and Current Biodiversity Legislation)
chunks.text: Key features, including as modified by the 2023 amendment, include (subject to verification of current rules made under the amended Act): • A requirement that certain categories of persons (in particular, foreign individuals/entities, and non-resident Indians, and entities not qualifying as Indian companies under the Companies Act, 2013 definition) obtain prior approval from the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) before accessing Indian biological resources or associated traditional knowledge for research, commercial use, bio-survey, or bio-utilization. • Under the 2023 amendment, Indian entities/nationals covered under the relevant provision (Section 7 of the Act) generally need only register with the NBA (rather than obtain full prior approval) before obtaining an intellectual property right based on Indian biological resources or associated TK, though prior approval remains required before commercialization of that IP.

chunks.section: 6.5 Biological Diversity Act (and Current Biodiversity Legislation)
chunks.text: • The 2023 amendment also introduced decriminalization of most offences under the Act (replacing certain criminal penalties with monetary penalties), an exemption for codified traditional knowledge and its practitioners (e.g., registered AYUSH practitioners) from certain access-approval requirements, simplified compliance for Indian systems of medicine industry participants (including AYUSH-sector companies, startups, and MSMEs), and coverage of Digital Sequence Information (DSI) under access and benefit-sharing obligations. [VERIFY current implementing rules, since the amendment’s practical effect depends heavily on rules and notifications issued under it, which continue to be developed/updated.]

The NBA is the statutory body established under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, responsible for regulating access to Indian biological resources and associated traditional knowledge, approving (where required) access and benefit-sharing arrangements, and advising the Central Government on biodiversity-related matters, including matters relating to intellectual property rights over inventions based on Indian biological resources or associated traditional knowledge. It works alongside State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) and local Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs).

The Ministry of AYUSH is the Government of India ministry (a separate ministry since 2014 [VERIFY], having earlier existed as the Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, and later the Department of AYUSH) responsible for the development, education, standardization, quality control, and research promotion of Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa, and Homoeopathy. It collaborates with CSIR on TKDL and separately supports Ayurvedic pharmacopoeia standardization, licensing frameworks for Ayurvedic
drug manufacturing, and research bodies such as the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS).

chunks.section: 6.8 Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
chunks.text: CSIR is India’s premier chain of national industrial research and development laboratories/institutions, functioning as an autonomous body under the (nominal) chairmanship of the Prime Minister of India, with a Director-General as executive head, administratively linked to the Ministry of Science and Technology. CSIR has played the lead technical role in creating and maintaining TKDL, and has historically been the institution that filed prior-art challenges in landmark cases such as the turmeric patent re-examination (Section 10).
(Cross-reference: see Section 3 for full treatment.) TKDL is jointly run by CSIR and the Ministry of AYUSH as a defensive prior-art database of Indian traditional medicinal knowledge.

The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations, headquartered in Geneva, responsible for administering a number of international IP treaties (e.g., the Paris Convention, the Berne Convention, the Patent Cooperation Treaty), promoting international IP policy cooperation, and — of direct relevance to this document — hosting the Intergovernmental Committee on Intellectual Property and Genetic Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Folklore (IGC), which has for many years been negotiating possible international instrument(s) on the protection of traditional knowledge, traditional cultural expressions, and genetic resources (see Section 9).

Section 6 Summary India’s Ayurveda/TK/IP-relevant institutional framework runs through the Indian Patent Office and CGPDTM (patents, under the Patents Act, 1970 and Patents Rules), the National Biodiversity Authority (biological-resource access, under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended in 2023), the Ministry of AYUSH (traditional- medicine regulation and standardization), CSIR (research and TKDL), and, internationally, WIPO (treaty administration and ongoing TK-protection negotiations). This section describes a general research workflow a researcher can use to investigate whether an Ayurvedic formulation or traditional practice may already exist as prior art. It is written as a practical, step-by-step method. All examples below are hypothetical and are labelled as such; they do not describe any real formulation, product, or patent.

Write a precise, technical description of exactly what is being investigated: what is the active ingredient or combination, what form is it in (powder, extract, oil, tablet), what is the claimed use, and what (if anything) is claimed to be new about it (a specific extraction ratio, a specific delivery method, a specific combination). Hypothetical example: “A proposed formulation combining an aqueous extract of Plant X with an aqueous extract of Plant Y, in a 3:1 ratio, delivered as an oral tablet, claimed to be useful for supporting joint comfort.”

List every active and inactive ingredient by both common/vernacular name and, where possible, botanical (Latin binomial) or chemical name, since patent and traditional-knowledge literature may use different naming conventions.

For each ingredient, research how it has traditionally been used, in which traditional medicine system(s), for what purpose, and in what form, using classical texts, TKDL (where accessible), and published ethnobotanical/ethnopharmacological literature.

Compile a list of all known synonyms for each ingredient and use-concept: Sanskrit, Hindi, regional-language names, older/obsolete botanical names (plant taxonomy is periodically revised, so an old scientific name may appear in older literature), and common English descriptive terms.

chunks.section: 7.5 Step 5 — Search Scientific Names of Plants
chunks.text: Search using the currently accepted botanical name and any historically used synonymous botanical names, since prior-art documents may predate a taxonomic reclassification.

If the traditional formulation has a classical or market name (e.g., a named classical Ayurvedic compound formulation), search for that name specifically, as well as for its individual ingredients, since the named formulation itself may appear directly in patent or TKDL prior art.

Search patent databases (see Section 8 for detailed search-concept guidance) using the ingredient names, synonyms, use-terms, and relevant classification codes (IPC/CPC), across multiple jurisdictions (India, USPTO, EPO, WIPO’s PATENTSCOPE, and others as relevant), since a relevant patent may be filed in a jurisdiction other than India.
Where accessible, search TKDL (Section 3) and any other relevant public traditional-knowledge or ethnobotanical databases, using the same ingredient/synonym/use-term list developed in Steps 2–6.

For every document found, record: what exactly is disclosed, in what form, using what ingredient(s) and use-claim, and the disclosure’s date. Assess how closely the disclosed subject matter matches the invention being investigated (Step 1).

Keep a structured, dated record of every search performed (search terms, databases used, date of search, and results), and archive copies of every relevant prior-art document found, with full bibliographic/publication details. This record is essential if the research is later used to support or oppose a patent application.

Compare the closest prior art found against the specific claims of the invention being investigated (not just its general subject area), and assess whether the invention as claimed would likely be considered new and non-obvious in light of that prior art — bearing in mind the Indian-law exclusions discussed in Section 5.4 (e.g., Sections 3(d), 3(e), and 3(p) of the Patents Act) if the analysis concerns patentability in India specifically.

chunks.section: 7.12 Step 12 — Consult a Qualified Patent Professional When Necessary
chunks.text: This workflow supports preliminary research and does not replace professional advice. Any decision to file a patent application, oppose someone else’s application,

chunks.section: 7.12 Step 12 — Consult a Qualified Patent Professional When Necessary
chunks.text: or rely on a novelty assessment for a commercial decision should involve a registered patent agent/attorney qualified in the relevant jurisdiction(s). Section 7 Summary A structured, twelve-step workflow — from precisely defining the invention through ingredient/synonym/name searches across both patent and traditional- knowledge databases, to recorded, dated evidence and professional consultation — supports a defensible assessment of whether an Ayurvedic formulation or practice may already exist as prior art. All worked examples in this section are hypothetical. Sources / Further Reading (Section 7) • WIPO — Patent search guidance and PATENTSCOPE: https://patentscope.wipo.int • Indian Patent Office — InPASS (Indian Patent Advanced Search System): https://ipindiaservices.gov.in • CSIR-TKDL Unit: https://www.csir.res.in/en/documents/tkdl
The specific words or phrases used to search a database — should include technical, common, and traditional/vernacular terms relevant to the subject matter.

Alternative words or names with the same or closely related meaning (e.g., different regional names for the same plant); a thorough search always tests multiple synonyms, since indexing and terminology vary by source and era.
A search technique using logical operators to combine or exclude keywords precisely.

• AND — narrows results to documents containing all specified terms (e.g., “turmeric AND wound”). • OR — broadens results to documents containing any of the specified terms (e.g., “turmeric OR Curcuma longa”). • NOT — excludes documents containing a specified term (e.g., “neem NOT cosmetic,” to exclude a particular use category).

Standardized alphanumeric codes assigned to patent documents describing their technical subject matter, allowing searches by technology area rather than only by text/keyword — important because keyword searches can miss relevant documents that use different terminology for the same concept.

A hierarchical, internationally standardized classification system (administered under a WIPO-linked international agreement) used by most patent offices worldwide, organizing all technology into sections, classes, subclasses, groups, and subgroups.

A more granular classification system jointly developed by the European Patent Office and the USPTO, based on the IPC but with additional subdivisions, now used by a number of major patent offices in addition to or instead of pure IPC coding.
Searching for patents by the name of the company or institution that owns (or will own) the patent rights, useful for tracking a specific competitor’s or research institution’s patent portfolio.
Searching for patents by the name(s) of the individual(s) credited as inventor, useful for tracking a specific researcher’s body of patented work.

The set of related patent applications/patents filed in multiple countries for the same underlying invention (typically via the Paris Convention priority route or the Patent Cooperation Treaty, PCT), sharing a common priority claim; useful because the same invention’s protection status can differ country by country.

The unique identifier assigned to a patent application or granted patent when it is officially published by a patent office (distinct from the application number and, once granted, from the grant/patent number in some jurisdictions).
The unique identifier assigned to a patent application at the time of filing, used to track it through the examination process.

The earliest filing date that an applicant is entitled to claim for assessing novelty and inventive step — typically the filing date of the first application for the same invention in any Paris Convention member country, which subsequent applications (filed within the priority period, typically 12 months for patents) can claim the benefit of.
The actual date on which a specific patent application was filed at a specific patent office.

The date on which a patent application (or, separately, a granted patent) is made publicly available by the patent office — commonly around 18 months after the priority date for applications, unless earlier/later publication rules apply.

The date on which a patent office formally grants the patent, after which enforceable exclusive rights generally begin (subject to jurisdiction-specific rules on provisional/interim rights between publication and grant).

The current standing of a patent application or patent (e.g., pending, granted, refused, withdrawn, lapsed for non-payment of renewal fees, revoked following opposition) — an essential thing to check, since an expired, lapsed, or revoked patent generally no longer restricts use of the invention (though the underlying disclosure remains valid prior art for other purposes).

The numbered statements at the end of a patent document that legally define the precise scope of the exclusive right being sought or granted; these — not the general description or the abstract — are what is compared against an accused product/process in an infringement analysis, and what is compared against prior art in a novelty/inventive-step analysis.
The detailed technical explanation in a patent document of what the invention is, how it works, and (per the sufficiency-of-disclosure requirement, Section 5.3.4) how to make and use it.

A short summary (typically around 150 words, subject to jurisdiction-specific limits) at the start of a patent document, intended for quick technical orientation; the abstract itself does not define legal claim scope.

Any documents (patents, scientific articles, books, and other public disclosures) predating the relevant priority/filing date that are relevant to assessing novelty and inventive step, as introduced in Section 5.6. Section 8 Summary Effective patent searching relies on combining precise keywords and synonyms with Boolean logic (AND/OR/NOT), classification-code searching (IPC/CPC) to catch documents using different terminology, and targeted assignee/inventor/family searches — while correctly reading bibliographic data (application/publication/priority/filing/grant dates and legal status) and focusing substantive comparison on the patent’s claims rather than its abstract or description alone. Sources / Further Reading (Section 8) • WIPO — IPC guide: https://www.wipo.int/classifications/ipc/en/ • Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC): https://www.cooperativepatentclassification.org • Indian Patent Office — InPASS search portal: https://ipindiaservices.gov.in

(Cross-reference Section 6.10.) WIPO administers major IP treaties and hosts ongoing negotiations specifically relevant to TK — the Intergovernmental Committee on Intellectual Property and Genetic Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Folklore (IGC). [VERIFY — recent development] In May 2024, WIPO member states adopted the WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge — a treaty requiring patent applicants to disclose the country of origin (or source) of genetic resources, and of associated traditional knowledge, used in an invention, where the claimed invention is materially based on such resources/knowledge. As with any treaty, its practical effect depends on the number and identity of ratifying countries and on national implementing legislation;
current ratification status should be checked on WIPO’s official treaty-status page before being relied upon.

chunks.section: 9.2 TRIPS (Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property
chunks.text: Rights) A World Trade Organization (WTO) agreement (in force since 1995) setting minimum standards for IP protection and enforcement that WTO member countries must implement in their national law, including minimum patent-term (20 years from filing) and patentable-subject-matter standards. TRIPS itself does not contain a dedicated regime for traditional knowledge protection, which is part of why TK protection has instead been pursued through separate instruments and negotiations (this section) and through defensive national tools like TKDL (Section 3).

A multilateral environmental treaty (opened for signature 1992, in force since 1993) with three main objectives: conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising from the use of genetic resources — including, under Article 8(j), a specific call for parties to respect, preserve, and maintain the knowledge, innovations, and practices of indigenous and local communities relevant to biodiversity conservation, and to encourage equitable sharing of benefits from their utilization.

A supplementary agreement to the CBD (adopted 2010, in force since 2014) that provides a more detailed legal framework for the effective implementation of the CBD’s access and benefit-sharing (ABS) objective, requiring parties to establish clear domestic measures on prior informed consent, mutually agreed terms, and benefit- sharing for access to genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge. [VERIFY India’s specific implementing measures and any updates, as domestic ABS rules are refined periodically — see Section 6.5 on the Biological Diversity Act framework, which is India’s principal domestic implementation route.]

Beyond the CBD/Nagoya (biodiversity-access) track, a separate but related international discussion — centered in WIPO’s IGC — has for many years explored whether and how to create dedicated international legal instrument(s) specifically protecting traditional knowledge and traditional cultural expressions as IP-like subject matter (as opposed to only regulating access to associated biological resources). As of this document’s preparation, this IGC process has produced the 2024 WIPO treaty noted in 9.1 (on disclosure obligations); broader substantive protection of TK and traditional cultural expressions themselves remains under continued negotiation. [VERIFY current status, as this is an active, evolving negotiation.]

The principle and set of legal mechanisms (rooted in the CBD and elaborated by the Nagoya Protocol) requiring that access to genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge be subject to prior informed consent from the providing country/community and mutually agreed terms, and that benefits arising from subsequent use (monetary — e.g., royalties — and non-monetary — e.g., capacity building, technology transfer) be shared fairly with the resource/knowledge provider.

Legal and administrative measures designed to prevent third parties from obtaining IP rights (typically patents) over subject matter that is not genuinely novel because it is already traditional knowledge — without necessarily creating any new proprietary right for the TK holder. TKDL (Section 3) is the paradigm example of a defensive-protection tool; the WIPO 2024 treaty’s disclosure-of-origin requirement (9.1) is a defensive measure operating at the international treaty level.

Legal measures that go further than defensive protection by creating actual enforceable rights for traditional knowledge holders/communities themselves — for example, requiring benefit-sharing agreements as a legal precondition for use (as under the Biological Diversity Act and Nagoya-type ABS frameworks), or (in some countries, though not comprehensively in India as of this document) dedicated sui generis statutory rights specifically for TK holders analogous to conventional IP rights. Positive protection is generally considered legally and institutionally harder to design than defensive protection, given the collective, often-oral, and continuously-evolving nature of much TK (see Section 2.4).

chunks.section: 9.9 How These Concepts Relate to Traditional Medicinal Knowledge
chunks.text: For Ayurveda specifically, the practical interaction of these frameworks is: • CBD/Nagoya + India’s Biological Diversity Act govern access to the biological resource (the plant/organism itself) and associated TK for research or commercial use, and require benefit-sharing. • TRIPS + national patent law (India’s Patents Act) govern whether a resulting invention can be patented, and Indian law specifically excludes bare traditional-knowledge “inventions” (Section 5.4). • WIPO’s IGC process and the 2024 disclosure-of-origin treaty operate at the international patent-procedure level, aiming to make sure patent offices worldwide are told where a claimed invention’s genetic resources/TK came from, supporting both defensive challenge and benefit-sharing enforcement.

chunks.section: 9.9 How These Concepts Relate to Traditional Medicinal Knowledge
chunks.text: • TKDL operates as a practical, searchable, defensive tool sitting underneath all of the above, helping ensure that patent examiners can actually find the relevant traditional-knowledge prior art in practice. Section 9 Summary International protection of TK associated with Ayurveda involves at least three separate legal tracks: biodiversity-access law (CBD, Nagoya Protocol, India’s Biological Diversity Act), conventional IP/trade law (TRIPS, national patent law and its TK-specific exclusions), and a still-developing dedicated TK-protection track at WIPO (culminating so far in the 2024 disclosure-of-origin treaty), with defensive tools like TKDL providing the practical, on-the-ground mechanism that connects TK documentation to real-world patent examination.

chunks.section: 10.1 Case Study — The Turmeric Patent Case
chunks.text: • Case name: University of Mississippi Medical Center — U.S. Patent No. 5,401,504, “Use of Turmeric in Wound Healing” • Country: United States (dispute originated from India’s challenge) • Approximate year: Patent granted 1995; re-examination requested 1996; patent revoked 1997 • Traditional knowledge involved: The use of turmeric (Curcuma longa) powder, administered both orally and topically, for wound healing — a use widely documented as traditional practice in Indian households and in Ayurvedic and other traditional literature. • IP issue: Novelty and obviousness — whether a patent claim on an already- traditionally-known use can be valid. • What was claimed: A patent (granted March 1995) covering a method of promoting wound healing by administering turmeric to a patient, orally and/or topically, along with associated exclusive commercial rights.

chunks.section: 10.1 Case Study — The Turmeric Patent Case
chunks.text: • What happened: India’s Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) filed a request for re-examination with the USPTO in 1996, submitting documentary prior art — reported to include roughly 32 references in Sanskrit, Hindi/Urdu, and other sources, along with a 1953 paper in the Journal of Indian Medical Association — demonstrating that turmeric’s wound-healing use was long-standing traditional and documented knowledge, not a new invention. • Final outcome: The USPTO rejected all claims on re-examination and formally revoked the patent (order dated in late 1997), on the ground that the claimed use was anticipated by prior art and therefore not novel/was obvious. • Why the case is important:

chunks.section: 10.1 Case Study — The Turmeric Patent Case
chunks.text: • Why the case is important: It is the most frequently cited example demonstrating that Indian traditional knowledge, if properly documented and presented as prior art, can defeat a wrongly granted patent — and it was the direct catalyst, along with the neem case below, for the creation of TKDL (Section 3), since it showed the cost and difficulty of fighting such patents after grant rather than preventing them beforehand.

chunks.section: 10.2 Case Study — The Neem Patent Case
chunks.text: • Case name: European Patent No. 0436257 (US Department of Agriculture / W.R. Grace & Co., later assigned to Thermo Trilogy) — neem-seed-derived fungicide • Country: Europe (European Patent Office, Munich); dispute involved U.S. and Indian parties/campaigners • Approximate year: Patent granted 1994/1995; opposition filed 1995; revoked by EPO Opposition Division in 2000; final appeal decision 2005 • Traditional knowledge involved: The use of neem (Azadirachta indica) seed-derived extracts as an antifungal/pesticidal agent — a use widely documented in Ayurvedic literature and long-standing Indian agricultural and medicinal practice. • IP issue: Whether the claimed invention (a specific method of controlling fungi on plants using a neem-oil formulation with defined hydrophobic- extract content) was novel and involved an inventive step, given the traditional and prior scientific record of neem’s antifungal use. • What was claimed:

chunks.section: 10.2 Case Study — The Neem Patent Case
chunks.text: • What was claimed: A patent covering a method of controlling fungi on plants by contacting the fungi with a neem-oil formulation containing a specified percentage range of a hydrophobic extract. • What happened: A legal opposition was filed in 1995 by environmentalist Vandana Shiva’s Research Foundation for Science, Technology and Ecology, together with the International Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements (IFOAM) and Magda Aelvoet (then a Member of the European Parliament), arguing the patent was not a genuine invention because neem’s fungicidal properties had been used in India for centuries; evidence included

chunks.section: 10.2 Case Study — The Neem Patent Case
chunks.text: ancient Ayurvedic textual references and testimony/prior scientific publications on neem’s antifungal effects. • Final outcome: The EPO’s Opposition Division revoked the patent in May 2000, finding it lacked novelty and inventive step; the patentees appealed, and the EPO’s Technical Board of Appeal dismissed the appeal in March 2005, upholding the revocation of the patent in its entirety. • Why the case is important: Widely described as the first case in which a patent was revoked at the EPO on grounds directly connected to biopiracy/traditional-knowledge prior art; it is cited internationally, alongside the turmeric case, as a foundational example motivating TKDL’s creation and broader international attention to defensive TK protection.

chunks.section: 10.3 Case Study — The Basmati Rice / RiceTec Dispute
chunks.text: • Case name: RiceTec Inc. — U.S. Patent No. 5,663,484, “Basmati Rice Lines and Grains” • Country: United States (dispute involved India as the objecting/affected country; Pakistan also has a strong interest in Basmati as a shared-origin product) • Approximate year: Patent granted September 1997; formal objection by India (via the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority, APEDA) around 2000; claims narrowed thereafter • Traditional knowledge involved:

chunks.section: 10.3 Case Study — The Basmati Rice / RiceTec Dispute
chunks.text: Basmati is a long-grain aromatic rice traditionally grown for generations in specific regions of India and Pakistan (the Indo-Gangetic plain/foothills of the Himalayas), and traditionally bred/selected by farmers in that region; the case is often discussed alongside TK cases because it involves a claim over a name and rice lines closely tied to traditional regional agricultural knowledge and practice, though it is more precisely framed as a geographical-indication and plant-related patent dispute than a medicinal-TK dispute. • IP issue: Whether a U.S. company could obtain patent rights over rice lines bred by cross-breeding traditional Basmati varieties with an American long- grain variety, including claims broad enough to potentially extend the “Basmati” name/characteristics to rice grown outside the traditional region, raising both patent-novelty and geographical-indication concerns. • What was claimed:

chunks.section: 10.3 Case Study — The Basmati Rice / RiceTec Dispute
chunks.text: • What was claimed: The original patent, as granted, included 20 claims covering rice lines and grains, some of which were broad enough to be read as covering “basmati” hybrid rice grown anywhere in the Western Hemisphere. • What happened: Following objections raised by the Indian government and public pressure/protest in India, and after India submitted supporting material, RiceTec voluntarily withdrew a substantial number of claims, and a U.S. Patent and Trademark Office re-examination certificate cancelled a number of the remaining claims relating specifically to rice matching the traditional Basmati description.

chunks.section: 10.3 Case Study — The Basmati Rice / RiceTec Dispute
chunks.text: • Final outcome: RiceTec was left holding a narrower patent covering only its own specifically bred rice lines/hybrids (commonly referenced varietal names include Bas867, RT1117, and RT1121), and the patent’s title was correspondingly narrowed; RiceTec was not permitted to claim general rights over rice simply because it was marketed using the term “Basmati” in a manner that misappropriated the geographic term’s traditional meaning. • Why the case is important: It is one of the most cited examples of how a poorly scrutinized patent claim can threaten a country’s traditional agricultural export identity, and it strongly informed India’s subsequent push to strengthen its Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, and to register Basmati and other traditional products as GIs domestically and, where possible, internationally.

chunks.section: 10.4 Case Study — The Kani Tribe and the Jeevani Benefit-Sharing Model
chunks.text: (TBGRI) • Case name: Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute (TBGRI) / Kani tribe — “Jeevani” formulation and benefit-sharing trust • Country: India (Kerala) • Approximate year: Traditional-knowledge collaboration began in 1987; product (“Jeevani”) developed and ready to market by around 1994–1996; benefit-sharing trust established mid-1990s; later difficulties documented through the 2000s • Traditional knowledge involved: Knowledge of the Kani tribe (an indigenous community of the Western Ghats/Agasthya Hills region) regarding the anti-fatigue and restorative properties of the Arogyapacha plant (Trichopus zeylanicus), traditionally consumed by Kani guides during long forest journeys. • IP issue:

chunks.section: 10.4 Case Study — The Kani Tribe and the Jeevani Benefit-Sharing Model
chunks.text: • IP issue: Whether and how a research institute could commercialize a formulation derived from tribal traditional knowledge, and how to structure a fair benefit-sharing arrangement with the source community, in a period (research began before the 1993 entry into force of the CBD) predating most formal ABS legal frameworks. • What was claimed: TBGRI researchers, guided by Kani informants, identified and studied the plant’s properties over roughly eight years of research, ultimately developing “Jeevani,” a polyherbal formulation combining Arogyapacha with three other traditionally used plants (ashwagandha, Piper longum, and Evolvulus alsinoides). • What happened: TBGRI licensed the manufacturing/marketing rights to the Arya Vaidya Pharmacy (AVP) of Coimbatore in exchange for a license fee (commonly reported as approximately Rs.

chunks.section: 10.4 Case Study — The Kani Tribe and the Jeevani Benefit-Sharing Model
chunks.text: 10 lakh) and a royalty (commonly reported as approximately 2% of ex-factory sales), and TBGRI agreed to share these proceeds equally with the Kani community through a dedicated trust. Implementation later encountered significant difficulties: disputes arose over raw-material collection rights (because Arogyapacha was not

chunks.section: 10.4 Case Study — The Kani Tribe and the Jeevani Benefit-Sharing Model
chunks.text: classified as a “minor forest produce” that the Kani could legally collect and sell, leading to conflicts with the forest department and, per some reports, cases against tribal collectors), and separately, an unrelated U.S. distributor of AVP products registered “Jeevani” as a trademark in the United States in 1999 without the involvement of TBGRI or the Kani community. • Final outcome: The arrangement is widely described as a pioneering, internationally cited early model of benefit-sharing predating most formal legal ABS requirements, but subsequent reporting (including from the 2000s) documented that the underlying trust fund became financially strained over time and that practical benefits to the Kani community were more limited and harder to sustain than initially envisioned, illustrating the real-world implementation challenges of benefit-sharing arrangements even when well- intentioned at the outset. • Why the case is important:

chunks.section: 10.4 Case Study — The Kani Tribe and the Jeevani Benefit-Sharing Model
chunks.text: • Why the case is important: It is commonly presented as both (a) a positive, early example of a research institution proactively sharing commercial benefits with a traditional-knowledge-holding community, and (b) a cautionary illustration that a benefit-sharing agreement’s practical success depends heavily on complementary legal clarity (e.g., forest/resource-access law) and long-term institutional follow-through, not just the initial agreement.

chunks.section: 10.5 Case Study — Hoodia Gordonii and the San Peoples’ Benefit-Sharing
chunks.text: Agreement • Case name: South African San Council / Working Group of Indigenous Minorities in Southern Africa (WIMSA) — CSIR (South Africa) Hoodia Benefit- Sharing Agreement • Country: South Africa (with regional relevance to San communities in Namibia, Botswana, Angola, and Zambia) • Approximate year: CSIR (South Africa) research and patenting activity from the 1990s; benefit-sharing agreement signed March 2003 • Traditional knowledge involved: Traditional knowledge of the San peoples of the Kalahari Desert regarding the use of the Hoodia gordonii plant to suppress hunger and thirst on long hunting trips, and for other traditional purposes (including for stomach pain and eye infections). • IP issue:

chunks.section: 10.5 Case Study — Hoodia Gordonii and the San Peoples’ Benefit-Sharing
chunks.text: • IP issue: South Africa’s Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR — a different institution from India’s CSIR, sharing only the acronym) isolated an appetite-suppressing compound (referred to as “P57”) from Hoodia and pursued patent protection and commercial licensing (to Phytopharm, a UK firm, which in turn licensed rights to Pfizer for further development) without initially involving, informing, or compensating the San, despite the underlying discovery relying directly on San traditional knowledge of the plant’s properties. • What was claimed: CSIR (South Africa) filed a patent application (national filing in South Africa in 1997, followed by a PCT international filing in 1998)

chunks.section: 10.5 Case Study — Hoodia Gordonii and the San Peoples’ Benefit-Sharing
chunks.text: covering pharmaceutical compositions extracted from Hoodia with appetite- suppressant activity. • What happened: After the San learned of the commercialization and patenting activity — reportedly including a moment in which the licensee’s representatives believed the San no longer existed as a people — the South African San Council, supported by WIMSA and non-governmental organizations, asserted the community’s traditional-knowledge rights and entered into negotiations with CSIR, citing South Africa’s obligations under the CBD and (then-emerging) international benefit-sharing norms. • Final outcome:

chunks.section: 10.5 Case Study — Hoodia Gordonii and the San Peoples’ Benefit-Sharing
chunks.text: • Final outcome: After roughly three years of negotiation, CSIR and the South African San Council signed a benefit-sharing agreement in March 2003, under which the San would receive a share of royalties (commonly reported as 6% of royalties received by CSIR from Phytopharm) and a share of milestone payments (commonly reported as 8% of certain milestone payments), paid into a trust established for community development purposes (education, training, and related upliftment programs) and intended to benefit San communities across the wider Southern African region, not only in South Africa. • Why the case is important:

chunks.section: 10.5 Case Study — Hoodia Gordonii and the San Peoples’ Benefit-Sharing
chunks.text: • Why the case is important: It is one of the most widely cited early examples of a formal, negotiated access and benefit-sharing agreement reached after a patent had already been filed/commercialized, illustrating both that meaningful benefit-sharing remedies are achievable even after the fact, and the structural limitation that such after-the-fact remedies typically capture only a fraction of the value generated, reinforcing the case for prior- informed-consent requirements (as later strengthened by the Nagoya Protocol — Section 9.4) rather than only after-the-fact negotiation.

chunks.section: 10.5 Case Study — Hoodia Gordonii and the San Peoples’ Benefit-Sharing
chunks.text: Section 10 Summary Five well-documented cases illustrate the recurring dynamics of traditional- knowledge-related IP disputes: two successful defensive challenges to wrongly granted patents (turmeric, neem); one dispute over a traditional agricultural name and its patent/geographical-indication implications (Basmati/RiceTec); and two benefit-sharing arrangements with a traditional-knowledge-holding community, one negotiated proactively before major commercialization (Kani/Jeevani) and one negotiated reactively after commercialization had already begun (Hoodia/San). All five cases directly informed the development of defensive protection tools (TKDL) and access/benefit-sharing law (CBD, Nagoya Protocol, and India’s Biological Diversity Act). This section describes the intended end-to-end workflow for the AyurIP Sahayak AI research assistant, from a user’s question to a sourced answer.

User Query → Query Understanding → Keyword/Synonym Expansion → Knowledge Base Retrieval → Patent/Traditional Knowledge Retrieval → Evidence Ranking → Context Construction → LLM Response → Source/Citation Display

The process begins with a natural-language question or request from the user (e.g., a researcher, student, patent professional, or Ayurveda practitioner), which may be broad (“What is TKDL?”) or specific (“Is a formulation combining ingredients A and B for use C likely to face novelty objections in India?”).

The system analyzes the query to determine: the query’s intent category (definitional/conceptual question, procedural/how-to question, case-law/precedent question, or novelty-assessment-support question); the specific entities mentioned (plant names, formulation names, legal provisions, institutions); and any ambiguity requiring clarification before proceeding (e.g., “Ayurveda” used generically vs. a specific classical formulation name).

Using the principles in Section 7 (Steps 2–6) and Section 8, the system expands the query’s key entities into a broader search-term set: botanical synonyms, vernacular- language names, alternative transliterations, related legal-provision references, and related classification codes — to avoid missing relevant material due to terminology mismatch, which (as discussed in Section 5.5) is precisely the structural problem that historically allowed wrongful patents to be granted.

The system retrieves the most relevant sections/chunks of this knowledge-base document (and any other configured internal knowledge sources) using the expanded term set, prioritizing self-contained sections (as this document is structured to support — see Section 12) so that retrieved chunks make sense on their own.

Where the query concerns a specific prior-art or novelty question, the system separately queries external/connected patent-search and traditional-knowledge resources (e.g., patent-office search portals, TKDL where access is available, scientific literature databases), following the step-by-step methodology in Section 7.

Retrieved material (from both Stage 4 and Stage 5) is ranked by relevance to the specific query and, where applicable, by authoritativeness of source (e.g., an official Patents Act provision or a primary patent-office decision should be weighted above a secondary blog summary), and by recency where the query concerns current legal rules (per this document’s general verification approach — see the Important Accuracy Rules in the document introduction).

The system assembles the highest-ranked, most relevant evidence into a coherent context for the underlying language model, structured to make clear which statements are: (a) traditional claims, (b) scientifically established facts, (c) current legal rules (with a verification flag where appropriate), and (d) case-study historical facts — mirroring the labeling conventions used throughout this document.

The underlying language model generates a response strictly grounded in the assembled context, following this document’s core accuracy rules: no fabrication of laws, cases, statistics, organizations, patents, or dates; clear distinction between traditional claims and scientific evidence; no medical diagnosis, treatment
instruction, or unsupported disease-cure claims; and explicit flagging of any point requiring independent verification.

The final response is presented to the user together with clear citations back to the specific source section/document/provision relied upon, so the user can independently verify any point before relying on it — consistent with this document’s overall design purpose as a RAG source that supports, rather than replaces, professional legal and scientific verification. Section 11 Summary AyurIP Sahayak’s workflow moves from raw user query through query understanding and synonym/keyword expansion, to parallel retrieval from this knowledge base and from external patent/TK databases, through evidence ranking and carefully labeled context construction, to a grounded LLM response that always displays its sources — designed throughout to prevent fabrication and to keep traditional, scientific, and legal claims clearly distinguished.
